title: Load Balancers
description: Understand how load balancers distribute traffic and keep applications available.

data.text: When an application becomes popular, a single server can no longer handle all the traffic. Load balancers sit in front of a pool of servers and distribute incoming requests across them. They improve performance, prevent overload, and ensure that if one server fails, traffic continues flowing to the healthy ones.

Load balancers operate at different layers of the network stack. Some make decisions based on IP addresses and ports, while others inspect the actual application content. Choosing the right type and algorithm is one of the most important infrastructure decisions you will make.

A load balancer maintains a list of healthy backend servers called a pool. For each incoming request, it selects one backend using a predefined algorithm. It also continuously checks whether backends are alive. If a server stops responding, the load balancer stops sending it traffic until it recovers.

data.title: Load Balancing Algorithms
items: Round Robin — sends each new request to the next server in the list. Simple and fair.
Least Connections — sends traffic to the server with the fewest active connections. Best for long-lived requests.
IP Hash — maps a client IP to a specific server. Useful for session affinity without sticky cookies.
Weighted Round Robin — servers with more capacity receive proportionally more traffic.
Least Response Time — combines active connections with recent latency to choose the fastest server.

data.text: Layer 4 load balancers operate at the transport layer. They see IP addresses and ports but cannot inspect the actual HTTP request. They are fast and simple, but they lack the intelligence to route based on URLs, headers, or cookies.

Layer 7 load balancers operate at the application layer. They can inspect the HTTP path, host header, or request body. This enables advanced routing: /api requests can go to API servers, /images to a CDN, and /admin to a protected pool. Layer 7 is more flexible but uses more CPU and memory.

data.title: Health Checks Are Critical
data.text: A load balancer is only as good as its health checks. If checks are too aggressive, healthy servers get removed during brief blips. If they are too lenient, failed servers keep receiving traffic. Always tune intervals and thresholds for your application's tolerance.

terms.definition: Also called sticky sessions. Ensures requests from the same client always reach the same backend server.
A periodic probe sent to backends to verify they are responsive and ready for traffic.
A backup server that takes over only when the primary fails, rather than sharing traffic continuously.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Load balancers distribute traffic across backends to improve availability and performance.
Algorithms range from simple Round Robin to adaptive Least Response Time.
Layer 4 is fast and simple; Layer 7 is powerful and flexible.
Health checks and timeouts must be tuned carefully to balance stability and responsiveness.
data.takeaway: Load balancing is not just about splitting traffic — it is about maintaining a healthy, responsive system under unpredictable real-world load.
